newsitem.title: USA: Moderate growth, moderate inflation fuel markets.
newsitem.headline: Moderate growth, moderate inflation fuel markets.

text.p: The government on Thursday painted another picture of moderate economic growth and stable inflation, helping convince Wall Street that the Federal Reserve will hold interest rates steady next week.

The latest batch of data -- showing industrial output gaining and consumer prices up just slightly in July -- provided more of the best-of-both-worlds news that has powered recent rallies in financial markets and allowed central bank policy-setters to leave interest rates unchanged for now.

"This is an economy that continues to experience moderate growth," said Bill Sullivan, chief money market economist at Dean Witter Securities. "We remain relatively free of any adverse consequences for the inflation picture."
Sullivan said the figures "put absolutely no pressure" on the Fed to adjust short-term interest rates at an interest rate policy meeting scheduled for Tuesday.
Stocks and bond prices responded favorably to the reports.
Shortly after 1 p.m., the Dow Jones industrial average was up more than 10 points at nearly 7,940 after moving up to even higher levels earlier in the day.
The inflation-sensitive 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was up more than three-quarters of a point, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, fell to 6.56 percent from 6.63 percent Wednesday.

A key factor behind the markets' euphoria was the Labor Department's report revealing only a modest 0.2 percent increase in the prices consumers paid for goods and services last month. The small rise matched Wall Street forecasts.

Production at the nation's mines, factories and utilities rose modestly in July as a drop in light truck manufacturing partly offset gains in aircraft and high-technology output, according to a Federal Reserve Board report.
Industrial production rose a slim 0.2 percent last month, as Wall Street economists had expected, after rising 0.3 percent in June, the Fed said.

The capacity use rate, which measures how close to production limits businesses are operating, slipped to a less-intense 83.1 percent from a revised 83.3 percent in June. The Fed had previously estimated the June rate at 83.5 percent.
In another report, the Commerce Department said inventories held by businesses took their biggest jump in more than two years in June, mostly because of a bulge in unsold goods held by wholesalers.
But economists played down the news, given the strength of the economy, which is in its seventh year of uninterrupted growth.

"It's not unusual for the economy to be building inventories when it's this strong," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc. in St. Louis. "It's not a problem until retail sales wane."
A separate report by the Labor Department showed the number of Americans claiming first-time jobless benefits in the week ended Aug. 9 rose by 12,000 to 316,000.
In the consumer price report, a drop of 0.1 percent in energy prices had a moderating effect on the overall price gains in July.

July food prices rose 0.3 percent, while grocery store prices also rose 0.3 percent, reflecting larger increases in the indexes for meats, poultry, fish, and other key food categories, the department said.
Apparel prices, up 0.2 percent, and transportation prices, which rose 0.1 percent in July, staged a rebound from June, when both areas had posted declines.
Analysts had expected the report to show few signs of inflation, saying businesses have been reluctant to push up prices despite mounting evidence of consumer confidence and plentiful jobs.
The producer price index released Wednesday showed wholesale prices falling for a record seventh consecutive month.
